pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Tsunamis — a very large, very fast ocean wave caused by an earthquake or volcanic eruption under the sea, which can cause great damage when it reaches land.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** In England this sits in KS2 **Geography** (physical geography: volcanoes and earthquakes and their effects), not KS2 science. Frame as a consequence of undersea earthquakes/eruptions, linked to the Geography hazards unit.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No dedicated elementary PE for tsunamis; the hazard connects to **2-ESS1-1** (some Earth events happen quickly) and to the earthquake/volcano patterns of **4-ESS2-2**. Reducing the impact of such hazards is the focus of **3-5-ETS1 / 4-ESS3-2** (design solutions to reduce impacts) — developed in the 9–11 'Earthquake-Resistant Design' topic. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisite is 'What Is an Earthquake' (and 'Why Earthquakes Happen'). Deliver the causal chain — undersea quake/eruption → huge fast wave → damage at the coast — and one counter-intuitive fact set: a tsunami is low and barely noticeable in deep ocean but rears up and piles onto the shore, and the sea often DRAWS BACK first as a natural warning. Keep tone matter-of-fact and safety-empowering, not frightening.
bestPractices: Teach the causal chain explicitly: something big moves the sea floor (earthquake or eruption) → the whole water column is pushed → a fast, long wave spreads out → it grows tall and floods when it reaches shallow coast.
Bust the 'giant surfing wave' image: in deep water a tsunami is low and fast; the danger is the enormous volume of water piling ashore, not a single tall curl.
Teach the natural warning sign as safety knowledge: if the sea suddenly pulls far back, move quickly to high ground — a concrete, empowering action.
Contrast a tsunami with an ordinary wind wave (wind waves are surface ripples; a tsunami moves the whole depth of water and carries vastly more energy).
Anchor with a real, age-appropriate case (e.g. a briefly told account) to make it real without dwelling on distressing detail; pair with the idea that warning systems now exist.
keyRepresentations: Side-view cross-section: sea-floor slip → wave low in deep water → wave rearing up over a shelving beach
Draw-back-then-surge sequence at the shoreline (the sea recedes, then floods in)
Comparison of a small wind wave vs a whole-depth tsunami wave
A fast-moving wavefront racing across an ocean map from an undersea quake to distant coasts
commonMisconceptions: A tsunami is one giant tall breaking/surfing wave (in deep water it is low; it grows and floods at the coast, often as a fast surge, sometimes a series of waves).
Tsunamis are caused by wind or storms (they are caused by sudden sea-floor movement — undersea earthquakes or eruptions, also landslides).
There is only one wave (tsunamis often arrive as several waves; later ones can be larger).
It's safe once the first wave passes / when the sea pulls back it's a chance to explore (the draw-back is a warning to flee; more water is coming).
Tsunamis are the same as ordinary tides (unrelated to daily tides; 'tidal wave' is a misleading old name).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach what a tsunami is and why it behaves so counter-intuitively: a sudden movement of the sea floor (undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption, also landslides) pushes the whole column of water, creating a low wave that races across the open ocean very fast and can reach distant coasts, then slows, stacks up tall and floods when it reaches shallow coast. Emphasise the safety-empowering natural warning signs: the sea sometimes drawing far back first (this does not always happen), and strong shaking near the coast. Contrast the whole-depth tsunami with an ordinary surface wind wave. Keep the tone matter-of-fact and reassuring (warning systems now exist), not frightening. In England this sits in KS2 Geography (physical geography hazards), not KS2 science.

activities.title: Set off the wave: watch it grow at the shore
feedback: If the learner expects a tall curling wave in deep water: point out that in deep water the tsunami is low and barely noticeable — the danger is the enormous volume of water piling ashore, not a single tall curl.
If the learner thinks a tsunami only affects the nearest beach: note that a low, fast tsunami can travel across a whole ocean and reach coasts far from where it started.
If the learner cannot say why it grows at the shore: replay the shallowing section and link slowing water to the wave stacking up higher.
Reinforce the cause: ask what had to move on the sea floor to start it — an earthquake or eruption, not wind.
activities.rationale: The counter-intuitive behaviour (low-and-fast across deep water, rearing up at the coast) is a process over space and time, so a driveable side-view the child triggers lets them see the growth-at-the-shore rather than just being told it. A static labelled diagram or a sequencing task can also convey the chain, but showing the motion makes the 'why does it grow?' concrete.
sourceClaims: Tsunamis are most commonly generated by undersea earthquakes (also volcanic eruptions and landslides); they travel very fast in deep water and grow tall in shallow coastal water.
learnerActions: Use a side-view cross-section of the ocean (deep water on one side, a shelving beach on the other) and trigger an undersea earthquake or eruption that moves the sea floor.

Watch the wave leave low and almost flat, racing across the deep ocean very fast; note a speed readout showing how quickly it crosses, and that it can spread right across the open ocean to reach distant coasts.
Watch what happens as the water gets shallow near the coast: the wave slows, stacks up and towers, then floods inland.
Predict out loud before triggering: 'Will the wave be tall out in the deep ocean, or will it grow near the shore?' Then check.
Describe the whole causal chain in your own words: sea floor moves → whole water column pushed → fast low wave spreads across the ocean → grows tall and floods at the shallow coast.
activities.intendedInsight: A tsunami is not a single tall surfing wave; it is the whole depth of water being pushed, staying low and fast as it spreads across deep ocean and only rearing up and flooding where the water becomes shallow at the coast.

activities.title: The sea pulls back: a warning to run
feedback: If the learner thinks the draw-back is a chance to explore or collect shells: explain the draw-back means much more water is coming — it is the signal to flee to high ground.
If the learner assumes one wave: tsunamis often arrive as a series; later waves can be larger, so stay away until officials say it is safe.
A safety card can snap up when the draw-back happens ('sea pulling back means run to high ground') to make the rule memorable.
activities.rationale: Teaching the natural warning sign as a concrete action turns frightening physics into empowering safety knowledge, and directly addresses the dangerous instinct to walk onto exposed sand. Seeing the draw-back motion makes the rule vivid, though the rule can also be taught and rehearsed verbally.
sourceClaims: A receding shoreline (the sea drawing back) is a natural tsunami warning sign; move immediately to high ground.
learnerActions: Watch the shoreline just before the surge arrives: in this example the water races OUT, exposing the sea bed, before flooding back in (this often happens, but not with every tsunami).
Answer: 'If you were at the beach and the sea suddenly pulled far back, exposing the sand, what would that mean and what would you do?'
Learn and repeat the safety rule: sea pulling back = get to high ground quickly; do not walk out onto the newly exposed sand.
Note that a tsunami can arrive as several waves, and later ones can be larger — it is not safe once the first wave passes.
activities.intendedInsight: A receding shoreline is a natural warning sign of an approaching tsunami; the correct, empowering response is to move immediately to high ground, not to explore the exposed sea bed. The sea does not always pull back first, so strong shaking near the coast or an official warning also means go to high ground.

activities.title: Wind wave vs whole-depth tsunami
feedback: If the learner says a tsunami is just a very big wind wave: show the depth comparison — wind waves move the surface, a tsunami moves water all the way down.
If the learner confuses tsunamis with tides: clarify they are unrelated to the daily tides caused by the Moon, and that 'tidal wave' is a misleading name.

Reinforce: tsunamis are caused by something suddenly pushing a huge amount of water, most often sea-floor movement in an undersea earthquake, and also eruptions or landslides. Ordinary wind does not make tsunamis.
activities.rationale: Contrasting the two wave types targets the common misconceptions that tsunamis come from wind/storms or are the same as tides, and makes the whole-depth idea concrete. The attached source claim supports the sea-floor cause element; the whole-depth/energy contrast is a qualified teaching inference, not a sourced fact. A live toggle makes the depth contrast visible; the contrast can equally be drawn or described.
sourceClaims: Tsunamis are most commonly generated by undersea earthquakes (also volcanic eruptions and landslides); they travel very fast in deep water and grow tall in shallow coastal water.
learnerActions: Compare a small wind-blown wave with a tsunami using a side-by-side toggle: the wind wave is a surface movement; the tsunami moves the whole depth of the water.
Explain in your own words how a tsunami is different from an ordinary wave at the beach.
Connect the difference to energy: because a tsunami moves the whole water column, it carries vastly more water and energy than a surface wave.
Identify the real cause of each: wind for ordinary waves, sudden sea-floor movement for a tsunami (and note a tsunami is unrelated to daily tides — 'tidal wave' is a misleading old name).
activities.intendedInsight: A tsunami differs fundamentally from a wind wave: wind waves are surface movements, while a tsunami moves the entire depth of the ocean and therefore carries far more water and energy.

activities.title: Make it real: a told account and warning systems
feedback: If the learner becomes anxious: emphasise the safety-empowering framing — warning systems and knowing what to do greatly reduce the danger.
Check the retell includes both the cause (sea-floor movement) and the warning (draw-back → high ground).
activities.rationale: A real case anchors the abstract process and motivates the safety knowledge, while pairing it with warning systems keeps the tone reassuring rather than frightening. A survivor or scientist account can motivate but does not by itself teach the wave mechanics, so it supports rather than replaces the process work.
sourceClaims: A receding shoreline (the sea drawing back) is a natural tsunami warning sign; move immediately to high ground.
learnerActions: Hear or read a brief, age-appropriate account of a real tsunami to understand that this really happens, without dwelling on distressing detail.
Discuss what people now do to stay safe: warning systems exist, and the natural signs (the sea drawing back, strong shaking near the coast) can give time to move.
Retell the causal chain and the safety rule to a partner or adult as if explaining it to someone who has never heard of a tsunami.
activities.intendedInsight: Tsunamis are real natural hazards, but people are not helpless: understanding the cause, recognising warning signs, and warning systems all help keep people safe.

constraints: Prerequisite understanding: 'What Is an Earthquake' and 'Why Earthquakes Happen' — frame the tsunami as a consequence of undersea earthquakes/eruptions.
Keep the tone matter-of-fact and safety-empowering, not frightening; pair real cases with the reassurance that warning systems now exist.

In England this topic sits in KS2 Geography (physical geography hazards), not KS2 science. In the US (NGSS) there is no dedicated elementary tsunami standard; it connects loosely to 2-ESS1-1 (some Earth events happen quickly) and 4-ESS2-2 (earthquake/volcano patterns), with hazard-impact reduction handled by engineering-design standards (3-5-ETS1 / 4-ESS3-2) in older grades. State-standard alignment was deferred in the source.

A sequencing or multiple-choice check (e.g. order the chain; 'what should you do if the sea pulls far back?'; 'how fast does a tsunami cross deep ocean?') can assess the cause, the speed/size facts and the safety rule; such recognition tasks check understanding but do not by themselves build the felt sense of the growth-at-the-shore and draw-back motion, which is better shown or enacted.

A 3D immersive bay view (rotatable run-up as the wave floods streets) can convey the spatial sweep inland as an extension, but the core teaching payload (low-in-deep, tall-at-shore, draw-back) is a cross-section story; choose the view that shows the depth and growth most clearly rather than assuming one format is inherently superior.
Address directly the dangerous instinct to explore the exposed sea bed when the sea draws back, and the belief that it is safe after the first wave.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all cited sources are marked verified:false in the row and were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source asserts a static image 'cannot show' the essential growth-at-the-shore and draw-back motion. This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the catalog ratings; it has been softened to note that showing motion makes the mechanism more concrete while diagrams and sequencing tasks can still teach the chain.
The source's 'fit' rankings (ideal/possible/poor) and format labels were catalog preferences; they are reframed as pedagogical options, not universal laws.

Speed readouts are presented qualitatively ('very fast'); the source gives no specific deep-ocean speed figure, so no numeric value is taught. If a slider with a numeric speed is used, source a correct value first.
The whole-depth-vs-surface and energy contrast in Activity 3 is pedagogically sound but is not directly stated by any cited source claim; it is presented as a qualified teaching inference.

Safety guidance (draw-back → high ground; strong shaking near the coast; multiple waves) is presented as general knowledge consistent with the cited NOAA/ITIC claims; 'strong shaking near the coast' goes slightly beyond the cited claims, so confirm all safety messaging against current official/local guidance before classroom use.

probeDeeper: What has to happen on the sea floor to start a tsunami?
If you saw the sea suddenly pull far back and expose the sand, what would that mean and what would you do?
Is a tsunami tall out in the deep ocean, or does it grow when it reaches shallow water near the coast?
How is a tsunami different from an ordinary wind-blown wave at the beach?
assess.correctAnswer: Not quite — a tsunami isn't a single curling surf wave. It's caused by a sudden movement of the sea floor (an undersea earthquake or eruption) that pushes the whole column of water. It races across the ocean very fast, low in deep water, then piles up high at the coast as a fast-rising surge or series of waves. A warning sign is the sea DRAWING BACK, exposing the sea bed, just before it arrives.

errorPatterns.pattern: A tsunami is one giant curling wave like a surfer's wave
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's the whole water column pushed by the sea floor — low and fast at sea, rearing and flooding as a surge at the coast.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's one giant curling wave, like a huge surfing wave.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a single tall breaking crest rather than a surge or series.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tsunamis are caused by strong wind or storms at sea
errorPatterns.nextMove: It comes from an undersea earthquake or eruption moving the sea floor, not from wind.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's caused by very strong wind and storms.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes it to weather rather than sea-floor movement.

errorPatterns.pattern: There's no warning — it just appears (misses the drawback)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The sea often pulls back first, exposing the sea bed — that's the signal to get to high ground.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies there is any sign at the shore beforehand.

responseLevels.gap: Pictures a single giant surf wave and/or blames wind; no idea of the sea-floor cause.
responseLevels.full: Explains a tsunami is the whole water column pushed by sea-floor movement, low and fast at sea then piling up at the coast, and names the sea drawing back as a warning — rejecting the single-surf-wave picture.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a tsunami is a large, fast, dangerous wave from an undersea quake but keeps the single-curling-wave image or misses the water-drawback warning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lots of people picture a tsunami as one giant curling wave, like a huge version of a surfing wave, appearing out of nowhere at the beach. Is that what a tsunami is really like? What causes it, and what might you notice at the shore just before it arrives?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can say 'a tsunami is a big dangerous wave' yet keep the surfing-wave picture and miss both the sea-floor cause and the tell-tale withdrawal. Asking about the cause AND what precedes it separates the real mechanism from the Hollywood image.
